title: Do Africans speak "African"?
subtitle: There is no language called African. Glottolog lists more than 2,000 of them, in 43 families.

parts.text: Some people say a person speaks "African", as if the continent had one language. It has more than two thousand.
Glottolog, a reference database of the world's languages, lists 2,373 languages with Africa as their only macroarea.
Leaving out its placeholder entries and the sign languages it files apart, 2,264 remain; some of them are no longer spoken.
Both counts come from the database's data file, as read for this site.
Those 2,264 belong to 43 families, and another 15 are isolates with no known relatives.
The largest family, Atlantic-Congo, holds 1,407 of them, about 62%. Afro-Asiatic, which includes Hausa and Amharic, holds 313.
The World Factbook's entry for Nigeria lists English (official), Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo and Fulani, and then adds "over 500 additional indigenous languages".
English is marked official in 22 of the 54 countries, French in 20, Arabic in 12 and Portuguese in 6, according to the Factbook's wording.
Those counts are made on the Society page of this site, and leave out languages the Factbook marks only as regional or working languages.
An official language is the one the state uses for law and schools. It is not necessarily the one people speak at home.

gaps: Glottolog's boundary between a language and a dialect is a scholarly choice, and other databases give different totals. Some of the 2,264 are extinct or nearly so.
The count uses entries with Africa as their only macroarea; languages shared with another macroarea, such as Arabic, are not in it.
The Factbook writes languages differently from country to country: some entries list a dozen, others name none. Official-language counts use its wording and our reading of it.
